'''Marguerite Shue-wen Chang''' (張葉學文; June 21, 1923 – May 5, 2012) was a Chinese-born American research chemist and inventor, awarded the Federal Woman's Award in 1973 for her work in the [[Naval Ordnance Laboratory|United States Naval Ordnance Laboratory]], based in Maryland.

== Personal life ==

=== Early life ===
Marguerite Shue-wen Ye was born in [[Nanjing]] in 1923.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/B-001-001-346|title=Lesser-known Women. A Biographical Dictionary|last=Beverly E. Golemba|date=1992|publisher=Lynne Rienner Publishers|pages=[https://archive.org/details/B-001-001-346/page/n293 278]}}</ref> She earned a bachelor's degree in chemistry at [[Wuhan University]]. She earned a master's degree and a Ph.D. in [[organic chemistry]] at [[Tulane University]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Smith|first=Jane Griswold|date=Winter 1973|title=The Cakewinner Fallacy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pnokSlUsoEMC&q=%22Marguerite%20S.%20Chang%22&pg=PA31|journal=The Journal of Navy Civilian Manpower Management|volume=7|pages=31}}</ref> where she was an associate member of the [[Sigma Xi]] honor society.<ref>[https://tuarchives.tulane.edu/sites/default/files/tuarchives/yearbooks/jambalayayearboo63edit.pdf Jambalaya] 1958 (Tulane University yearbook).</ref> Her dissertation advisor was Joseph H. Boyer.

=== Adulthood ===
Marguerite S. Chang was married to George K. Chang.<ref name=":1" /> The couple moved to the United States together in 1946, and had two sons while Marguerite Chang was a graduate student at Tulane University. The Changs decided to stay in the United States after 1949.<ref name=":0" /> Marguerite S. Chang died in 2012, aged 88 years, in [[Palo Alto, California]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=June 8, 2012 |title=Notice of Petition to Administer Estate of Marguerite S. Chang |page=67 |work=Palo Alto Online |url=https://www.paloaltoonline.com/morguepdf/2012/2012_06_08.paw.section2.pdf |access-date=November 19, 2019}}</ref>

== Career ==
Chang moved to the United States in 1946. From 1959 she worked at the United States Naval Ordnance Laboratory in Maryland, developing [[propellant]]s for missiles and rockets, working on safety procedures for the manufacture and use of propellants.<ref name=":0" /> She was named as an inventor on several patents, assigned to the United States government between 1976 and 1986, for processes, production methods and chemical compositions.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://patents.justia.com/inventor/marguerite-s-chang|title=Marguerite S. Chang Inventions, Patents and Patent Applications|website=Justia Patents Search|access-date=2019-11-19}}</ref>

Chang's scientific publications included "The Identification of C<sub>32</sub>H<sub>20</sub>N<sub>4</sub>O<sub>8</sub>, a Product from [[Acetophenone]] and [[Nitric acid|Nitric Acid]]" (''Journal of the American Chemical Society'' 1960, with Joseph H. Boyer), and "Bis(cyclopropanecarbonyl)furoxan" (''Journal of Organic Chemistry'' 1968, with James U. Lowe Jr.).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chang|first1=Marguerite S.|last2=Lowe|first2=James U.|date=1968-02-01|title=Bis(cyclopropanecarbonyl)furoxan|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|volume=33|issue=2|pages=866–867|doi=10.1021/jo01266a092|issn=0022-3263}}</ref>
[[File:IsabellaKarleJohnWarnerMargueriteChang.jpg|alt=Isabella Karle, John Warner, and Marguerite Chang pose for a photo. Both women are holding awards. Karl is a white woman, smiling; Warner is a white man in a tuxedo; Chang is a Chinese woman with grey hair, smiling.|thumb|[[Isabella Karle]], [[John Warner]] (Secretary of the Navy), and Marguerite S. Chang, from a 1973 annual report of the [[United States Naval Research Laboratory|U.S. Naval Research Laboratory]].]]
Chang is included in Conversations 760-009 and 871-009 of the White House Tapes, in the [[Oval Office]] for a photo sessions with President [[Richard Nixon]] and others in August 1972 and March 1973.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nixonlibrary.gov/white-house-tapes/760/conversation-760-009|title=Conversation 760-009|website=Richard Nixon Museum and Library|access-date=2019-11-20}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nixonfoundation.org/artifact/tape-871-conversation-9-871-009/|title=Tape 871, Conversation 9 (871-009) » Richard Nixon Foundation|date=2016-08-26|website=Richard Nixon Foundation|language=en-US|access-date=2019-11-20}}</ref> She was one of the six women to receive the Federal Woman's Award in 1973.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=March–April 1973|title=6 Women Careerists Get Top Award|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NwH8h6wCerMC&q=%22Marguerite+S.+Chang%22&pg=RA1-PP1|journal=Equal Opportunity in Federal Employment|volume=5|pages=3}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|date=Spring 1973|title=Award Winners Meet the President|url=https://www.cia.gov/library/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP00-01458R000100020017-1.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170123005505/https://www.cia.gov/library/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP00-01458R000100020017-1.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 23, 2017|journal=Women in Action|volume=3|pages=1}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Robey|first=Marie|date=April–June 1973|title=Six Winning Women|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IzhmmrYlSIcC&q=%22Marguerite+Chang%22&pg=RA3-PA20|journal=Civil Service Journal|pages=19–20}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/CIA-RDP84-00313R000100250012-1|title=CIVIL SERVICE JOURNAL|last=Central Intelligence Agency|date=1969-09-01|location=Internet Archive|pages=[https://archive.org/details/CIA-RDP84-00313R000100250012-1/page/n122 3]}}</ref>
